2 Timothy 3: was the world “waxing worse” in Timothy's day?
Does 2 Timothy 3 describe the world just before a future rapture, and does verse 13 (“evil men will go from bad to worse”) mean history must keep declining?
The popular reading
Many prophecy books read the vice list of 3:1-5 as a portrait of our own culture, and verse 13 as a law that history must get worse until the end.
Timothy is told to avoid them
Paul ends the list with “avoid such people” (3:5). He could only say that if they were in Timothy's world.
The last days had begun
Hebrews says God spoke “in these last days” by his Son, and Paul says the ends of the ages had come on his readers. The last days were the closing days of the old covenant age.
Like Jannes and Jambres
Paul compares the false teachers to Pharaoh's magicians who opposed Moses: they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all.
Paul's own persecutions
The chapter is full of Paul's history: Antioch, Iconium and Lystra. Verse 13 describes the impostors who troubled him and Timothy.
The program: Scripture and good works
Paul's answer is not escape but Scripture, which equips the believer for every good work. That is a call to build.
Expectation shapes work
If believers are taught that decline is certain, they stop planning and building. Scripture's model is the ant, which prepares for what is ahead.
“Do business until I come”
The parable of the minas sits in the same chapter as Jesus weeping over Jerusalem and foretelling its siege. Many of his parables warned of the coming judgement on that city.

Futurists answer that 3:1 is phrased as future (“in the last days there will come times of difficulty”), and that verse 13 states a principle that deception grows over time. Many futurists are themselves active in evangelism and public life and reject the idea that their view forbids building.
2 Timothy 3 described the opponents of Paul and Timothy in the apostolic generation. It is not a forecast of inevitable decline, and it ends with a program of faithful, Scripture-equipped work.

Verse 12, “all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,” does state a lasting principle; this reading applies the decline of verse 13 to the impostors, not the persecution of verse 12.
Do Roman coins date the book of Revelation?
A coin of Domitian (about AD 82-83) shows his dead infant son on a globe surrounded by seven stars. Does it show that Revelation, with Christ holding seven stars, was written about AD 95?
The late-date claim
Some argue that Christ holding the seven stars (Revelation 1:16) answers this coin of Domitian's deified son, so Revelation should be dated to Domitian's reign.
Stars meant deification
On Roman coins a star, or stars, usually marked a ruler or family member declared divine after death. It was a standard design, not a one-off.
Seven stars long before Domitian
A crescent with seven stars appears on a Republican coin of about 76 BC, and seven stars honoured the deified Augustus on Cretan coins under Caligula and Claudius.
And long after him
The crescent and seven stars reappear under Hadrian (AD 125-128) and on coins of Julia Maesa in the 210s-220s. A design used for three centuries cannot point to one decade.
Revelation explains its own symbol
“The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches.” No coin is needed to decode it.
Stars as people in Scripture
Joseph's dream, Abraham's offspring and the woman crowned with twelve stars already use stars for people, and the prophets use falling stars for fallen rulers.
The number of the beast
“Nero Caesar” in Hebrew letters totals 666; without the final n it totals 616, a variant Irenaeus knew. That points to Nero, and to a date before AD 70.
The time words
Revelation says its events must soon take place. Something had to follow soon after it was written.
Republican denarius
Crescent moon with seven stars (L. Lucretius Trio).
DIVVS IVLIVS coin of Augustus
Caesar's comet as a sign of his deification (one star, not seven).
Caligula's coin of Divus Augustus
The deified Augustus shown with stars (usually two).
Cretan coins under Caligula and Claudius
Seven stars honouring the deified Augustus.
Domitian's coin of his dead son
The infant on a globe surrounded by seven stars: the coin cited for a late date.
Hadrian's denarii
Crescent and seven stars.
Julia Maesa's denarius
SAECVLI FELICITAS: crescent and seven stars.

Late-date scholars rest mainly on Irenaeus (about AD 180), who placed the vision near the end of Domitian's reign, and on the condition of the seven churches. For them the coin is background colour (Christ, not the emperor's son, holds the stars), not proof, and most admit it does not settle the date.

The coin does not date Revelation. Seven stars were a common deification design for three centuries, and Revelation defines its own stars. The Nero number and the “soon” texts fit a date before AD 70 better.
Josephus describes a sword-shaped star and a year-long comet over Jerusalem before its fall (Jewish War 6.5.3) but gives no year; linking it to Halley's comet of AD 66 is a modern suggestion.
Does the futurist reading of the Olivet Discourse hold up?
A widely read futurist book argues that Jesus mentions the temple's fall only in Matthew 24:2 and then answers questions about the end of history. Does the text support that?
The futurist claim
Jesus, it is said, “virtually ignores” the disciples' question about when the temple would fall, and describes a future, worldwide tribulation.
The question was answered
Nothing says Jesus ignored it. He told them the stones in front of them would fall before “this generation” passed.
A local escape
The tribulation can be escaped by fleeing from Judea to the mountains, which only makes sense for a local catastrophe.
Cosmic language, historic judgement
Sun and moon darkened and stars falling is the prophets' language for the fall of Babylon and of Judah.
Everywhere else in the Gospels it means Jesus' contemporaries, and many commentators who are not preterists agree.
“Near” means near
James explains “at hand” as “at the door”: close, not merely possible at any moment.
Literal signs, literally fulfilled
There were real earthquakes, famines and false prophets in that generation; preterism does not spiritualise them.
Paul says the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven; the word for world in Matthew 24:14 means the inhabited Roman world.

Futurists answer that the disciples asked two or three questions (the temple, his coming, the end of the age), that AD 70 was a preview of a greater fulfilment, that “generation” can mean “race” or the generation that sees the final signs, and that the gathering of the elect and Matthew 25's judgement go beyond AD 70.
The futurist reading has to set aside the time texts and the local instructions. A first-century fulfilment of the discourse remains the more natural reading.
Some partial preterists themselves see a shift to the final coming at 24:36 or 25:31; the Matthew 24 study shows both.
Who were the “last days” scoffers, and when?
Are the mockers of 2 Peter 3 and Jude modern sceptics of a soon return, or first-century opponents mocking Jesus' prophecy about his own generation?
Who gets called a scoffer today
Christians who question date-setting are often called the scoffers of 2 Peter 3. But the time words of Scripture (“soon,” “near,” “at the door”) are the real issue.
Jesus tied his coming to his generation
Some standing there would live to see it, and this generation would not pass until all these things happened.
Jude: “these are” the ones
Jude repeats the apostles' warning about mockers in the last time and then says, in the present tense, “these are” the ones causing divisions. The scoffers were already present.
What they mocked
“Where is the promise of his coming?” Decades after Jesus spoke, the temple still stood, recently completed and more splendid than ever.
Scoffers in Jerusalem before
Isaiah addressed “scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem,” and God's answer was a cornerstone laid in Zion, which the apostles apply to Christ.
The prophecy at the trial
Jesus told the high priest, “from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds.” Then the guards mocked him: “Prophesy!”
Last days of Jerusalem
The 17th-century scholar John Lightfoot read “last days” in these letters as the last days of Jerusalem and the Jewish state, while insisting the warning still applies to every generation.
The promise kept
The coming the scoffers mocked arrived in judgement on that generation, and the temple fell, as Jesus said.

Futurists answer that 2 Peter 3 links the coming to heavens and earth dissolved by fire and a new heavens and earth (3:7, 10-13), which sounds like the end of history; that “all things continue as they were” is a timeless sceptic's complaint; that “a day is as a thousand years” expects a long delay; and that many scholars date 2 Peter after AD 70.

The scoffers Peter and Jude warned about were first-century opponents who mocked Jesus' prophecy for his own generation. The label should not be turned on Christians who take the Bible's time words seriously.

2 Peter 3:10-13 is the hardest text for this reading, and partial preterists differ on it: many read it as the final judgement, some as the end of the old covenant world. The date of 2 Peter is also debated.
Why prophecy pessimism keeps returning
Why do so many Christians expect the world to get worse until the end, and what happens to a church that expects only decline?
Reading fulfilled prophecy as future
A major reason for recurring end-times fever is reading prophecies that were fulfilled in the first century as if they were still waiting to happen.
The first-century mistake
Many in Jesus' day failed to see him as the fulfilment of their own Scriptures; the reverse mistake is failing to see what he fulfilled.
What we expect shapes what we build
A church that expects only defeat stops planning and investing in the next generation, while others who expect an earthly future shape the culture.
The kingdom grows
Scripture's own pictures are of growth: a stone that fills the earth, a mustard seed, leaven through all the dough.
Christ reigns now
He must reign until all his enemies are under his feet; the believer's labour in the Lord is not in vain.

Premillennial and amillennial believers answer that hope rests on Christ's return, not on progress in history, and that many of them have built schools, hospitals and missions while expecting the world to be mixed or worse until the end.
Reading the prophecies in their setting removes the “everything must get worse” mood and frees the church to work with hope.
Claims about which groups will dominate the culture are predictions, not exegesis; the biblical point is the call to faithful work.
